public_brief: Our returns desk needs one function it can trust: refund_eligibility(category, days_since_delivery, condition). category is the product category string, days_since_delivery is an integer count of days since the carrier marked the order delivered (negative means it has not arrived yet), and condition is the customer-reported state of the item. The function hands back exactly one verdict string: 'full', 'partial', or 'denied'. Two input conventions are fixed and published: the only recognized conditions are 'new', 'opened', and 'defective', and anything else raises ValueError - that validation runs before any policy door, so even a final-sale category or an undelivered order with a bogus condition gets the exception, not a verdict; and an unrecognized category is never an error - it simply falls back to the standard treatment. Years of return policy have layered the rest on top of that shape - windows that vary by what was bought, states that grade a verdict down, a few hard doors that shut everything out - and I am deliberately not listing them in this ticket; the grader knows current policy and calls the function directly with everyday returns and deliberately nasty edge cases, comparing the verdict string that comes back. Keep it a pure function apart from that one validation raise: no printing, no prompting, no file or network access, and every other input gets a defined answer.
entry_contract: Implement refund_eligibility(category, days_since_delivery, condition) taking three positional arguments and returning one of the exact strings 'full', 'partial', or 'denied'; an unrecognized condition string raises ValueError before any policy is applied, while an unrecognized category is answered with the standard treatment rather than an error.

hidden_spec.rule: The standard return window is 30 days from delivery, counted inclusively: day 30 still earns a verdict from the window rules, day 31 is denied.
Category-specific windows override the standard: electronics shorten to 15 days and perishables to 7, while any category not on that list (known or unknown) uses the standard 30.
Within the window, condition 'new' earns 'full' while condition 'opened' grades down to 'partial'; being opened never extends the window.
A negative days_since_delivery means the order was never delivered and is 'denied' outright, even for defective items; day 0 counts as delivered and is judged normally.
Condition 'defective' earns 'full' up to 90 days after delivery inclusive, overriding the category window, and 'denied' past day 90.
Anything in the clearance category is 'denied' regardless of condition or timing - final sale stays final even for defective items.

Any condition string other than 'new', 'opened', or 'defective' raises ValueError, and that validation runs before every other rule, including the clearance and delivery checks; an unrecognized category never raises - it takes the standard-window treatment (both error-path conventions are published in the ticket).

answer_sheet.answer: Thirty days from delivery, and the thirtieth day itself still counts. Thirty-one is too late.
Electronics tighten to fifteen days and perishables to seven. Anything we didn't name - even a category we've never heard of - falls back to the standard thirty.
Inside the window, new is a full refund and opened grades down to partial. And no, opening the box doesn't buy you extra days.
Nothing refunds before it has arrived: negative day counts are denied even when the unit is defective. Day zero counts as delivered.
Defective units ride outside the category window - full refund any time up to ninety days inclusive, and denied once past ninety.
Clearance is final sale. Denied come what may - defects included, that's the deal with clearance pricing.
The only recognized states are new, opened, and defective. Anything else raises ValueError, and we validate before every other rule - even final sale doesn't get to answer first.
Out of scope - this returns a verdict only; the amount engine computes dollars somewhere else.
Out of scope - no labels or logistics here; that belongs to fulfillment.

provenance.derivation: Rules derived from mainstream retail return-policy conventions (30-day standard windows with category-specific exceptions, opened-vs-new condition grading, delivered-before-return prerequisite, 90-day defect coverage, final-sale exclusions, strict enum validation), not from any WiseCounsil design document. Round-3 calibration revision (2026-10-05): no conventions moved into or out of the brief - the two error-path conventions (strict condition enum raised before every policy door, unknown category answered with the standard treatment rather than an error) were already the published surface - and the hidden rules are unchanged; the tests were de-coupled instead, holding the condition-grading probe to a day every plausible window contains and moving the opened-does-not-extend probe to a day past every plausible window, so a wrong window guess now costs only the window tests instead of cascading through grading, delivery, and defect rules.
